newsitem.title: PANAMA: Size of Panama anti-drug facility hinges on U.S..
newsitem.headline: Size of Panama anti-drug facility hinges on U.S..

text.p: A possible international anti-drug centre in Panama could operate without U.S. participation but on a smaller scale, Panamanian President Ernesto Perez Balladares said on Tuesday.

"Without the United States, the centre would not be as ambitious as we have proposed," he told local RPC radio. "It could operate as a Latin American centre, an instructional centre, an intelligence centre, but obviously it wouldn't have be the same size as we envision it with the United States because the U.S. owns the specialised equipment."

The United States and Panama had held preliminary talks to turn Howard Air Base, at the Pacific entrance of the Panama Canal, into an international anti-narcotics centre. Howard runs about 8,000 counter-drug flights a year in the region.
The Panamanian leader did not say whether he had agreed to accept a U.S. military presence of some 2,000 personnel to operate the centre, as Monday's El Panama America reported.

"We are exploring this very seriously to ensure the centre would be truly effective and not a (military) base in disguise," he said. "We are working out a general agreement. We don't have a date but I believe this stage will conclude very soon."

The commander of U.S. forces in Latin America, Gen. Wesley Clark, said last month the planned centre would not "be a multinational institution," but all of its actions "would be taken by sovereign national forces."

Perez Balladares had repeatedly stated his unwillingness to negotiate a U.S. military presence in Panama in the next century. But he said the United States could keep Howard at no cost for use as an anti-drug centre.
Washington is to turn over control of the Panama Canal and withdraw all troops and bases by Dec. 31, 1999.
